(1) mutants of FIV were selected with the combination AZT and ddI; and (2) the mutants selected with AZT and ddC were cross-resistant to ddC, PFA, and ddI and were hypersensitive (i.e., 10- to 100-fold more susceptible) to ddC.

(1) the mutants of feline (and other retroviruses) which are selected in the presence (or absence) of ddC, AZT and/or ddI display a variety of phenotypes which include resistance to ddC, AZC and ddI, hypersensitivity to ddC and cross-resistance to PFA; and (2) these phenotypes are not necessarily correlated with the specific mutations which occur in the RT genes of these mutants.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an animal model system for the study of HIV infection and AIDS.
the development of a feline immunodeficient virus (FIV), which is a natural lentivirus that infects domestic cats.
the development of an in vivo model system for the study of the molecular mechanisms of drug action, drug resistance, and the pathogenicity of FIV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the selection of FIV mutants in the presence of AZT plus dideoxyinosine leads to mutants which are cross-resistant to PMA and are hypersensitive to 3'-deoxy-2',3'- didehydrothymidine.
the selection of drug resistant mutants of FIV is not dependent on the combination of AZTs and ddIs, but rather on the individual drugs used.
the mutants selected with ddI alone or in combination with AZT have a common phenotype, namely, resistance to ddI, hypersensitivity to ddC, and cross-resistance to PFA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the combination of AZI plus ddI does not provide any advantage in selecting mutants which are cross-resistant to these two drugs.
the combination of AZD and ddI is not synergistic, but rather that it is antagonistic in that the two compounds select for the same resistant mutants.
selection with ddI alone, AZT alone, or AZT plus ddC in cell culture results in FIV mutants with a 2-fold to 4-fold decrease in susceptibility.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not possible to select FIV mutants that are resistant to both AZT and ddI, and that the combination of AZ T and ddI does not provide a selective advantage to FIV mutants over the wild type.

the selection of FIV mutants with the combination of ddI and AZT does not lead to the generation of a mutant which has a phenotype different from that of mutants selected with ddI or AZT individually.
